name: Bad Religion
label: Epitaph
lede: Four high schoolers play hardcore in three-part harmony, and one of them starts a label to press the records. Epitaph is still his forty years on.

eras.title: Hardcore with harmonies, paid for by somebody's father
eras.text: Four high school kids from the Valley start Bad Religion in 1980. Gurewitz invents Epitaph to press the records, and his father's loan pays for a first album that sells around 10,000 copies.

years.cap: The first lineup at a USC fraternity party, November 20, 1980
years.src: Wikipedia: Brett Gurewitz · Wikipedia: How Could Hell Be Any Worse?
years.h: Bad Religion gets its name from a wish to "piss people off"
years.p: [[Greg Graffin|046f8f41-f788-4da6-905d-26d1856f676d]], [[Brett Gurewitz|cd40188b-ea30-4729-bebb-e8c5091c9d02]], [[Jay Bentley|5b2bf657-acc4-476e-b2f3-a72e417accf0]] and drummer Jay Ziskrout, all still in high school, start the band in Los Angeles in 1980. Graffin says the name came from that goal.
years.xp:
All four went to El Camino Real High School in Woodland Hills, according to Wikipedia's Gurewitz entry.

They were in a studio in North Hollywood on October 31 and November 1, 1980, and finished seven songs the first night. That session became their first album.

years.cap: Gurewitz on guitar at The Vex, East L.A.
years.h: Gurewitz starts Epitaph so the band has a way to press records
years.p: He founds the label in Los Angeles to put out Bad Religion's music. Forty years on, it is still his.

years.h: A six-song EP puts Epitaph's name on a record
years.p: The self-titled Bad Religion EP is the label's first release. Pete Finestone takes the drum stool from Ziskrout, who quits during the album sessions that follow.

years.cap: Bad Religion at The Vex, East L.A.
years.src: Wikipedia: How Could Hell Be Any Worse? · Wikipedia: Brett Gurewitz · Wikipedia: Bad Religion
years.h: Gurewitz's father lends $3,000, and How Could Hell Be Any Worse? gets made
years.p: The album runs 29 minutes 40 seconds and comes out on Epitaph in 1982. Wikipedia reports it sold roughly 12,000 copies.
years.xp:
Sales of the EP and a $3,000 loan from Gurewitz's father paid for the record. It was cut at Track Record in North Hollywood, over a first night in late 1980 and a weekend in January 1981. Ziskrout quit mid-session and Finestone finished it. Greg Hetson, not yet a member, played one guitar solo.

The front cover is an Edward Colver photograph; the back is a Gustave Doré illustration from Dante. Wikipedia's band entry puts first-year sales near 12,000, while its Gurewitz entry says 10,000.

Zack de la Rocha of Rage Against the Machine first heard it in 1985, at fifteen: "a defining moment for me."
play: How Could Hell Be Any Worse?

eras.title: Ten thousand out, eleven thousand back
eras.text: Graffin goes to keyboards, the rhythm section walks, and Gurewitz leaves for rehab. After a split in 1985, Graffin re-forms the band in 1986 with Greg Hetson of the Circle Jerks.

years.big: "Sent out ten thousand copies and gotten eleven thousand back."
years.src: Wikipedia: Into the Unknown · Wikipedia: Bad Religion
years.h: Into the Unknown trades the guitars for Graffin's synthesizer
years.p: Gurewitz's joke about the 1983 album, which has Graffin on keyboards and piano. Wikipedia says the band played its songs live once, for 12 people.
years.xp:
Bentley quit partway through the first track, objecting to the synthesizers, and Finestone left to study in England. Paul Dedona and Davy Goldman took bass and drums, the only players on a Bad Religion record besides the regulars. It was cut at Perspective Sound in Sun Valley.

Wikipedia says most copies were sold out of the warehouse without the band's knowledge. The Maximumrocknroll founder called it "slickly produced early '70s wimp rock"; AllMusic later called it "a terrific record." It stayed unreleased in any official format until the 2010 vinyl box set, 3,000 copies.

years.h: Gurewitz leaves for rehab and the band goes dark
years.p: Gurewitz exits in 1983 and goes into rehab for drug addiction, per Wikipedia. Epitaph and the band both stop.

years.h: Bad Religion calls it quits in mid-1985
years.p: After a stretch with [[Greg Hetson|42351137-7257-4529-be9a-57385d9a8ac0]] of the [[Circle Jerks|22995eba-1238-4b4f-a937-ac2c5767ab9f]] on guitar, the band splits, with Gurewitz in rehab and the members' lives pulling apart.

years.h: Graffin rounds everybody back up
years.p: Graffin re-forms Bad Religion in 1986: Bentley back on bass, Gurewitz back from rehab, Hetson and Finestone on guitar and drums.

eras.title: Suffer resets the clock
eras.text: The re-formed band makes the record fans trace the sound back to, and sales climb from there: more than 80,000 for No Control, then 100,000 for Against the Grain.

years.h: Three fanzines name Suffer album of the year
years.p: The first record since the re-form swaps the early years' noise for tight three-part harmonies at speed. Wikipedia lists Trust, Maximum Rocknroll and Flipside among the voters.

years.h: No Control outsells everything before it
years.p: Released in November 1989, it passes 80,000 copies, per Wikipedia, the band's best total to that point.
play: I Want to Conquer the World

years.h: Against the Grain is the first 100,000 seller
years.p: Wikipedia says the sales showed how fast the band was growing. The album holds "21st Century (Digital Boy)", generally regarded as its best-known song.

years.cap: Bad Religion on stage at the Country Club, Reseda, May 24, 1991
years.h: Schayer takes the sticks after Finestone's April exit
years.p: Drummer Pete Finestone leaves in April 1991, and [[Bobby Schayer|6d35d697-620b-42ec-ab32-6721e86502e7]] takes the kit.

years.h: Generator is cut almost live at Westbeach
years.p: The band records in the enlarged Westbeach Recorders studio, all playing together for the first time, per Wikipedia. "Atomic Garden" becomes its first music video.

eras.title: Atlantic calls and Gurewitz walks
eras.text: Bad Religion signs to Atlantic and charts for the first time, then loses its co-writer to the label he started, just as The Offspring take off.

years.src: Wikipedia: Recipe for Hate · Wikipedia: Bad Religion
years.h: Recipe for Hate debuts at No. 14 on the Heatseekers chart
years.p: Out June 4, 1993 on Epitaph and reissued by Atlantic that September, it is the band's first chart record. Eddie Vedder of Pearl Jam sings on "American Jesus".
years.xp:
Vedder also sings on "Watch It Die", and Johnette Napolitano of Concrete Blonde sings backing vocals on "Struck a Nerve". It was recorded at Westbeach and mixed at Brooklyn Recording Studios, and Wikipedia puts sales near 200,000.

Drummer Bobby Schayer compared the slide-guitar track "Man with a Mission" to Sgt. Pepper's. Author Dave Thompson called the record "a major league breakthrough."

years.h: Bad Religion plays L7's Rock for Choice benefit
years.p: The band is on the bill at the Hollywood Palladium on April 30, 1993.

years.src: Wikipedia: Brett Gurewitz · Wikipedia: Bad Religion
years.h: Gurewitz leaves to run Epitaph as The Offspring explode
years.p: Gurewitz exits in 1994, just before Stranger Than Fiction, to give the label his full time. Brian Baker of [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]] and [[Dag Nasty|4709dd69-1034-4634-9e88-d1099453b192]] replaces him.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says he left "to concentrate on the future of Epitaph" as The Offspring grew into one of the biggest bands of the mid-1990s.

Baker, who had also played in Junkyard, turned down a spot with R.E.M. to take the job. A live version of "21st Century (Digital Boy)" from Pinkpop 1995 shows the new lineup.

years.cap: Ticket for Bad Religion at the Erne club in Oiartzun, Spain, September 24, 1994
years.h: Stranger Than Fiction peaks at No. 87, then goes gold in 1998
years.p: Released in September 1994, with a re-recorded "21st Century (Digital Boy)" and Baker on guitar, it is the band's first for Atlantic. Gold came on March 4, 1998, for over half a million copies.

eras.title: Producers with famous names
eras.text: Ric Ocasek and Todd Rundgren take turns in the producer's chair, No Substance splits critics, and the band spends a summer opening arenas for Blink-182.

years.cap: Ticket for Bad Religion at Roseland, New York, April 17, 1996
years.h: Ric Ocasek of the Cars produces The Gray Race
years.p: The record gets a minor U.S. radio hit with "A Walk" but doesn't match Stranger Than Fiction's reception, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Critics and fans split on No Substance
years.p: Wikipedia says the 1998 Atlantic record drew mixed reviews from both, after the success of Stranger Than Fiction.

years.h: Three months of arenas as Blink-182's opener
years.p: The band opens a U.S. arena tour for Blink-182 in the summer of 2000.

years.big: "He met his idol, and he was a jerk!"
years.src: Wikipedia: Bad Religion · Wikipedia: Brett Gurewitz
years.h: Todd Rundgren produces The New America
years.p: Rundgren was an early Graffin influence. Bentley's recollection of the sessions, per Wikipedia: Rundgren "didn't like Greg and that made Greg so mad!"
years.xp: Gurewitz had been out of the band since 1994, but in 1999 he reunited with Graffin and co-wrote "Believe It" for the album.

years.cap: Ticket for Bad Religion at the Electric Factory, Philadelphia, October 21, 2000
years.h: A shoulder injury ends Schayer's run, and Wackerman steps in
years.p: Bobby Schayer leaves after a serious shoulder injury, and [[Brooks Wackerman|422763c1-9762-4586-b2a4-0a6f54ed254e]] of [[Suicidal Tendencies|e9e2a634-984f-4c10-bf7b-7970179e1ef1]] takes the kit.

eras.title: Back to Epitaph, angrier
eras.text: Atlantic lets go, Epitaph takes the band back and Gurewitz rejoins. The records that follow get louder about politics, and New Maps of Hell reaches No. 35.

years.src: Wikipedia: Bad Religion · Wikipedia: Brett Gurewitz
years.h: Atlantic lets them go; Epitaph takes them back
years.p: Dropped in 2001, the band returns to Epitaph and Gurewitz rejoins, though he has not toured since.
years.xp: Graffin on the 1994 split, per Wikipedia: "we never had any serious acrimony between the two of us." He admitted some disappointment when Gurewitz left.

years.h: Home again for The Process of Belief
years.p: The six-piece lineup records its first Epitaph release after the Atlantic split.

years.cap: Bad Religion at the House of Blues
years.h: Gurewitz is furious at Bush, and The Empire Strikes First sounds it
years.p: Out in June 2004, it is angrier and faster. Gurewitz called his anger at George W. Bush "the major inspiration" for it.

years.h: Epitaph reissues the first six albums, remastered
years.p: The April 2004 remasters arrive with the documentary DVD Along the Way. How Could Hell Be Any Worse? alone gains ten bonus tracks.

years.h: New Maps of Hell climbs to No. 35, their best chart showing so far
years.p: Released July 10, 2007, it spawns three singles: "Honest Goodbye", "Heroes and Martyrs" and "New Dark Ages". The band joins the 2007 Warped Tour.

eras.title: Thirty-four years in, a top-20 album
eras.text: Thirty shows in thirty nights mark the anniversary, True North becomes the first top-20 album, and guitar and drums change hands. Then 2020 cancels everything.

years.cap: Bad Religion live in Seattle, November 2010
years.h: Thirty nights at the House of Blues for thirty years
years.p: In March and April 2010 the band plays 30 shows in 30 nights at House of Blues venues in Southern California and Nevada, 30 songs a night.
years.xp: The anniversary also produced 30 Years Live, a free download released May 18, 2010.

years.h: The Dissent of Man lands at No. 35 on the Billboard 200
years.p: Released September 28, 2010, it also debuts at No. 6 on the Independent Albums chart, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Graffin turns his evolutionary biology PhD into a book
years.p: Anarchy Evolution, Graffin's book on faith, science and Bad Religion, comes out in 2010.

years.cap: Bad Religion at Ottawa Bluesfest, July 2012
years.h: Bad Religion headlines the Reason Rally in Washington
years.p: On March 24, 2012, the band shares the bill with Richard Dawkins, Tim Minchin, James Randi and Eddie Izzard.

years.h: True North reaches No. 18, a first for the band
years.p: Out January 22, 2013, it is their first top-20 album and their highest Billboard 200 peak in a 34-year career.

years.h: Hetson steps back and Dimkich fills in
years.p: Greg Hetson steps away from touring in May 2013. Mike Dimkich is confirmed permanent on January 11, 2014.

years.h: Bad Religion makes a Christmas record
years.p: Christmas Songs is the band's first holiday album.

years.h: Wackerman leaves for Avenged Sevenfold
years.p: Brooks Wackerman departs on October 27, 2015 after fourteen years. Jamie Miller, formerly of ...And You Will Know Us by the Trail of Dead, takes over.

years.h: Age of Unreason aims at Donald Trump
years.p: Announced February 26, 2019 and out May 3, the seventeenth album is driven by the band's disdain for Trump. Lead single "Chaos from Within" premieres the day it's announced.

years.h: The first year without a show since 1980
years.p: COVID-19 cancels every date in 2020. The authorised autobiography, Do What You Want, comes out August 18.
years.xp: Hachette Books published Do What You Want, the band's first authorised, participatory biography.

sources.title: Wikipedia: How Could Hell Be Any Worse?
